Ante ese panorama, empresas tecnológicas y laboratorios desarrollan sistemas que usan luz para transmitir información y reducir el calor de los equipos, una alternativa que podría disminuir la energía destinada a enfriarlos.
La tecnología se llama fotónica. En lugar de mover la información mediante señales eléctricas a través de cables de cobre, la transporta con luz por fibra óptica. La fibra ya se utiliza en las comunicaciones de larga distancia, pero ahora la industria busca incorporarla a las conexiones internas de estas instalaciones, entre servidores, procesadores y equipos de red.
“Creo que estamos llegando al final de la era del cobre”, afirmó Chris Sharp, director de Tecnología de Digital Realty, en declaraciones recogidas por la BBC. Con esa frase no sugirió que el metal dejará de utilizarse, sino que su peso en las conexiones internas podría disminuir.
Una instalación de 100 megavatios puede requerir unas 400 toneladas de cobre, según el medio británico. La mayor parte se destina a la red eléctrica y a los equipos de refrigeración; del total, unas 70 toneladas se usan en los servidores y cerca de 20, en el cableado que los conecta.

Sovereignty is a spectrum and not a one-size-fits-all approach
Sovereignty cannot be treated as a linear standard
Digital sovereignty today is less about where data sits and more about who controls it. It is the ability for organizations to govern their data, infrastructure and operations, while retaining the flexibility needed to innovate.
Sovereignty is about having true control over your data and knowing where it lives, how it is regulated and exactly how it can be accessed at all times. Organizations can approach sovereignty through balancing regulatory requirements, operational resilience and innovation.
Different industries face vastly different pressures when it comes to data sovereignty. Banks, insurers, and healthcare providers must protect sensitive data while staying agile, while tech companies or logistics firms often require a greater level of flexibility.
Principal Technologist, EMEA at MongoDB.
In plain terms, data sovereignty is impacted by how data is governed by the laws of the country or region it is physically stored and/or accessed in. Data ownership and control are crucial, but current conversations about sovereignty have become a catch-all for resilience and security – which goes beyond data residency alone. It is never just about the physical location of the data.
The main challenge organizations face now is how to determine the right level of sovereignty for their regulatory, operational and innovation specific needs.

articles.title: Syrian Hacker Behind Fake Tweet That Triggered $136 Billion Market Drop Gets 42 Months in Prison
articles.summary:
Ahmad Umar Agha, a Syrian Electronic Army hacker known online as "Th3Pr0," has been sentenced by a U.S. federal court to 42 months in prison for his role in a hacking conspiracy that targeted Western news outlets.
The conspiracy was organized and led by members of former Syrian President Bashar al-Assad's inner circle, including the commander of Syria's General Intelligence Directorate, the U.S. Justice Department said on October 29.
The pro-Assad Syrian Electronic Army began its attacks in 2011. Its members sent phishing emails to steal employees' passwords, then used those passwords to deface websites, redirect web traffic, and hijack social media accounts, according to a 2014 FBI affidavit.
On April 23, 2013, the group hijacked the Associated Press's Twitter account and posted a false report that President Barack Obama had been injured in two explosions at the White House.
Twitter's message confirming a password reset for that account was sent to a Gmail account used primarily by Agha, the affidavit says.
The Justice Department said Agha carried out that hack, which caused a temporary $136 billion drop in the value of stocks in the Dow Jones Industrial Average. Agha later told Business Insider that a big drop in the Dow "was our goal of that hack attack" and that "it was a big victory for us."
Agha was first charged in June 2014 in a complaint that remained secret until March 2016. That month, the FBI added him and co-defendant Firas Dardar to its Cyber's Most Wanted list …

articles.title: Why Urgent Security Fixes Aren't Fixed. Observe, Prove, Act, Confirm Gets Them Moving
articles.summary:
The alert is critical. The fix is known. And the ticket sits in a queue for days. Security teams understand the risk, but the people who keep applications available need proof that the change won’t break anything.
Their concerns are practical. An IPS protection could block legitimate traffic. A configuration change could interrupt a service. An endpoint policy could affect an application the business depends on. Without evidence, the recommendation waits.
Safe remediation answers that hesitation with evidence. It tests the proposed action against your environment, applies the approved change, and confirms the result. Security and operations teams decide together, with facts.
The Cost of Leaving Protection in Detect
Many organizations already own protection they don’t enforce. Signatures sit inactive or in Detect mode while teams weigh false positives, inspection capacity, and business continuity. Meanwhile, applications and traffic patterns change, exceptions pile up, and policies drift away from how the environment runs today.
In the Safe Remediation white paper, 47% of the organizations measured had less than 50% protection enablement. Much of the capability they need is already in their environments.
Turning everything on isn’t the answer. Every activation carries risk. Teams need to know which changes matter for a given exposure, and how each will behave in production today.

This leaves a shortage of memory for consumer devices such as computers and phones, which is driving up costs for device manufacturers.

articles.title: Un musée et ses visiteurs piégés par l'IA de Google, qui l'annonçait fermé à tort !

L’aperçu IA de Google a annoncé à tort la fermeture du Centre Juno Beach, en Normandie, jusqu’en mai 2027. Le musée du Débarquement a démenti, mais corriger l’IA de Google s’est avéré bien plus compliqué que prévu.
Le Centre Juno Beach de Courseulles-sur-Mer, près de Caen, dédié au Débarquement, a découvert à ses dépens qu'une IA de Google pouvait informer sur la fermeture d'un musée sans demander l'avis de personne. En pleines vacances de la Toussaint, le résumé généré par le moteur de recherche annonçait une fermeture totale des lieux jusqu'en mai 2027, de quoi semer le doute chez les visiteurs. articles.title: WinRAR en LEGO : ce projet cache une excellente blague sur sa période d’essai
articles.summary:
Les célèbres livres d'archive de WinRAR ont inspiré un projet déposé sur LEGO Ideas. Derrière la sangle de l’archiveur, trois petites scènes racontent le fonctionnement du logiciel, avec un clin d’œil à cette licence dont tant d’utilisateurs ont repoussé l’achat.
Trois livres violet, bleu et vert, une sangle marron et une boucle métallique : même sans le nom du logiciel, les habitués de Windows devraient reconnaître l’icône. Sur LEGO Ideas, le créateur carlos_silva94 propose de la transformer en objet à exposer sur un bureau ou dans une bibliothèque. Mais l’intérêt de cette construction se trouve aussi à l’intérieur.
Une compression très physique et un responsable des licences endormi
Chacun des trois volumes dissimule une scène miniature. Dans celui consacré à la compression, un ouvrier emploie une méthode assez éloignée des algorithmes : il s’assoit sur les fichiers pour les faire tenir dans moins de place. Le deuxième compartiment accueille un archiviste, occupé à trier et ranger des informations dans des boîtes.
Le troisième réserve la meilleure plaisanterie. Dans le bureau chargé de valider les licences, l’employé s’est endormi à son poste. Une manière d’expliquer pourquoi la période d’essai de WinRAR ne semble jamais vraiment prendre fin : le responsable a tout simplement cessé de s’en occuper.
La plaisanterie est connue de longue date, mais WinRAR n’est pas gratuit pour autant : la période d’essai dure officiellement 40 jours, après lesquels une licence est nécessaire.…

'Not great' shopping agents still have a long way to go

- Jassy says the AI agent experience is still "not great"
Amazon CEO Andy Jassy has said he is not worried about the effect of AI-powered shopping agents such as Meta Muse, saying the services are still "not great".
Speaking after the company revealed yet another set of record financial results, Jassy told analysts barely any customers are using shopping agents as the experience is “still not great, nor more convenient than coming to a retailer directly.”
Jassy’s comments followed Amazon's decision to block Meta's new AI assistant, Muse, from accessing its online store in September 2026, claiming this would violate the conditions of use its customers have agreed to.
Muse is not doing the business...yet
Since its launch in September 2026, Muse has proven popular with customers, despite several examples of the service accessing information it was not supposed to.
